vignette: Elias first sits in my office on a quiet Tuesday morning, his boots planted flat on the floor, shoulders squared toward the door. He is thirty-four, of African descent, and carries a stillness that feels practiced rather than peaceful. The story he brings me begins on a rain-slicked evening eighteen months ago, in an apartment he still avoids driving past. He was thirty-three. The argument starts over nothing concrete, but what stays with him is the exact moment the air changes: the way his ex-partner's breathing shifts, the sudden stillness in her shoulders, the first hard impact against his jaw. He does not describe it as a single incident. He describes it as a curriculum. He learns, over weeks, to map the geometry of danger: which floorboards creak before a strike, how to keep his phone within arm's reach, how to make himself small enough to survive the night. He leaves when he can. He tells no one. Today, he navigates a different kind of territory. He works as a state parole officer, a job that requires him to read rooms, manage risk, and hold steady boundaries with people who are often testing them. He brings that same hyper-awareness home. When his current partner, Julian, reaches across the coffee table to hand him a mug, Elias's breath stops. He watches the hand move in slow motion, his ribs tightening, his stomach dropping, before his mind catches up and labels the movement harmless. He places his palms flat on his knees. He breathes until his shoulders unclench. He tells himself he is overreacting. He knows he is. His sleep is fractured. He lies awake at 2 a.m., heart drumming against his sternum, convinced he hears the familiar cadence of footsteps in the hallway. He wakes with a dry mouth and the phantom pressure of a heavy hand on his chest. He stops sleeping on his back. He sleeps on his side, facing the bedroom door, one hand resting on the nightstand beside a flashlight and his work radio. He deletes old photographs. He changes his phone passcode twice this month. When a colleague at the parole office mentions "family stuff" near the breakroom copier, Elias turns off his radio and walks out, claiming he left his notes in the car. He didn't. He just needs the open space, the fluorescent lights, the predictable structure of a uniform and a badge. At least there, power is written down. At least there, he does not have to guess when the mood will turn. His work changes in quiet ways. He used to move through supervision meetings with a steady rhythm, offering resources, setting limits, matching tone to tension. Now, when a parolee leans forward across the desk, Elias's posture locks. His voice flattens into official cadence. He logs more field visits than necessary, telling himself it is about compliance, but really he needs the wide spaces, the clear sightlines, the physical distance that keeps him safe. He misses the version of himself that could sit comfortably in a room without scanning for exits. Julian tries. He leaves encouraging notes on the fridge. He asks gentle questions that Elias deflects with dry humor. Elias loves him, and the love sits beside the fear like two heavy coats. He watches Julian's hands with the same wary precision he once reserved for his ex. He wonders, sometimes, if intimacy is just another form of surrender. He stops himself from apologizing for breathing too loud. He stops himself from flinching when Julian laughs suddenly in the next room. He sits very still, as if stillness might keep him safe. When our session ends, Elias stands, adjusts his tie, and checks his watch. He mentions a morning court report, then nods toward the door. "See you next week," he says, his voice even, his posture composed. In the hallway, I watch him walk away. His steps are measured. His breathing is steady. For now, that is enough.
